title: Passover: four children
hookLine: the wise, the wicked, the simple, and the one who doesn't know how to ask
tomorrow: Passover: it would have been enough

cards: Anyone who's explained something to a room knows this moment. You've told the story, and now the questions come. One person asks something sharp and detailed.
One rolls their eyes: why does anyone bother? One just says, wait, what is this? And one says nothing at all, and you can't tell if they're lost or bored or shy.

The Torah tells parents four separate times to explain the Exodus to a child. The rabbis noticed the four verses don't match, and from that they built a whole page of the Haggadah, the book read at the seder.

teach.b: The Haggadah says the Torah speaks of four children: one wise, one wicked, one simple, and one who doesn't know how to ask. Each gets a different answer.
The wise child asks about all the testimonies, statutes and laws God commanded, so you teach them the laws of Passover, down to the last detail of the night.

teach.h: THE WICKED: FOR ME, NOT HIM.
teach.b: The wicked child asks, what is this service to you? To you, the Haggadah notices, not to him.
He's stepped out of the circle, so the answer is blunt, a verse in the old Jewish translation: "It is because of that which the LORD did for me when I came forth out of Egypt." For me, not for him.
Strong words, and Jewish teachers have argued about them for centuries. Many say the point is that even this child is at the table, and still gets an answer. The simple child asks, what is this?
So you answer simply: with a strong hand, God brought us out of Egypt, from the house of slavery. And the one who doesn't know how to ask?

teach.h: THE SILENT: YOU OPEN IT UP.
teach.b: You open it up for them. You start the conversation.
In the Hebrew, that you is feminine, at, and some take it as a hint that this child is often helped first by a mother. The page gives no single right way to tell the story.
You tell it to the person in front of you, at their level. Four children, four answers, one table.

how: At the seder, after the Four Questions, the Haggadah's passage of the four children is read aloud, and many families discuss it, sometimes using illustrated Haggadot that picture the four children in very different ways.

o: the festival remembering the Exodus from Egypt
the day the Torah was given at Mount Sinai
the autumn harvest festival of living in booths

games.q: inside the four children — tap the pairs.
p: taught all the laws of the night
asks what it means to you
you open it up for them

s: the four children come from four different Torah verses
the Torah tells parents to explain the Exodus four times, in four ways.
the Haggadah sends the wicked child away from the table
he gets an answer; many teachers stress he's still at the table.
the one who doesn't know how to ask gets no answer
you open it up for them; you start the conversation.

games.q: a child at the seder sits silent. they haven't asked anything all night. what does the Haggadah say to do?
o: give them the laws in full.
games.why: you open it up for them. the one who can't ask doesn't have to; the telling starts with you.

practice: Think of someone who asked you something lately: a child, a coworker, a friend new to something you know well. Were they sharp, skeptical, confused or silent?
Picture answering them again at their level: more detail, fewer words, or a door opened for the question they didn't know to ask.

wordCard.voice: Passover. The festival of leaving Egypt, and a story told four ways, to four children. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: you, open for him. the 'you' is in the feminine form.

carryVoice: Your line: answer each child. A week of things turned upside down: two gifts, masks, clearing out, a candle, a plate that speaks, and four children. That's day six hundred seventy-nine.

sources.q: It is because of that which the LORD did for me when I came forth out of Egypt.
